name: Steppe
notes: Cold, semi-arid temperate grassland of feather grasses, fescues and wormwoods with rare shrubs, treeless except ravines; Eurasian steppe (Ukraine to Mongolia) with Patagonian and Great Basin analogues.

canopy.name: Siberian elm
canopy.origin: Central Asia, Mongolia and N China
canopy.source: Ulmus pumila, Central Asia/Mongolia/N China steppe ravines and river banks, 10-25 m — Flora of China

traits.native_range: Ulmus pumila, Central Asia/Mongolia/N China steppe ravines and river banks, 10-25 m — Flora of China
traits.leaf_shape: simple or compound broad leaves, most deciduous in cold bands
traits.trunk: single trunk dividing into a rounded crown
traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

canopy.silhouette: open rounded crown of small leaves, brittle limbs

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal: two small oblong cotyledons, then alternate, small (2-5 cm), singly toothed, almost symmetrical elm leaves on a thin zigzag stem. Saplings are fast, slender whips, often growing 1 m or more a year, with short side shoots in two flat ranks; browsed or cut stems resprout into bushy multi-stemmed clumps. The open, rounded crown forms after 10-15 years.
growth.source: Wikipedia (Ulmus pumila): to 25 m, rarely over 60 yr in N America but 100-150 yr (one over 250) in its native range, not shade-tolerant; USDA Woody Plant Seed Manual (Ulmus): flowers Mar-Apr, fruit ripe and shed Apr-May, seed-bearing from age 8, fresh seed germinates 81-96% with no pretreatment. Height curve estimated from its fast early growth.

fruiting.source: USDA Woody Plant Seed Manual (Ulmus): flowers Mar-Apr before the leaves, samaras 10-14 mm ripe and dispersed Apr-May; Wikipedia: flowers about 3 mm with brownish-red anthers, bloom one week, samaras whitish tan, orbicular, wind-dispersed; young samaras are eaten raw or steamed in N China. Cluster size, fruit set, hang and rot times and crop estimated.

canopy.name: Wild apple
canopy.source: Malus sieversii, the wild ancestor of the domestic apple, a 5-12 m tree of the foothill forest-steppe and ravines of the Tian Shan and Dzungarian Alatau (Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Xinjiang) at 900-1800 m — Kew POWO / Forsline et al. 2003 / Flora of China
canopy.silhouette: low round-headed apple tree in a steppe ravine

growth.juvenile_note: Seeds need a winter's cold before they sprout. The seedling is a thin single stem with downy, finely toothed oval leaves; browsing and drought make many young trees bushy and several-stemmed. Old trees are low and wide with a short scaly trunk and heavy, crooked limbs, standing in groves in the gullies of the foothills.
growth.source: Forsline et al. 2003, Collection, maintenance, characterization and utilization of wild apples of Central Asia (trees to 10-12 m, some estimated at up to 300 yr; fruit 1-8 cm, yellow-green to red; groves at 900-1600 m); Flora of China. Juvenile period and growth estimated from Malus.

fruiting.source: Forsline et al. 2003 and Flora of China Malus sieversii (white to pink flowers in May; apples 2-8 cm, very variable in colour and taste, ripen Aug-Sep and fall; eaten and spread by bears, boar and horses). Crop estimated.

bark.notes: grey-brown bark flaking in small thin scales; crooked heavy limbs

leaf.notes: oval finely toothed leaves, downy and pale beneath

flower.form: white flushed pink five-petalled blossoms in clusters with the leaves

fruit.form: small to medium apples, yellow-green to red, very variable

appearance.seasonal: deciduous; pink-white spring blossom, yellow in autumn
appearance.silhouette: low round apple trees scattered down a grassy ravine
appearance.refs: Kew POWO; Flora of China; Forsline et al. 2003

canopy.name: Russian olive
canopy.source: Elaeagnus angustifolia, a thorny silver-leaved tree 4-10 m of river valleys, tugai and saline flats from the Caucasus and southern Russia through Kazakhstan and Mongolia to western China; nitrogen-fixing, salt- and drought-tolerant — Kew POWO / Flora of China / USDA FEIS

leaf.note: narrow lance-shaped leaves covered in silvery scales, especially beneath

canopy.silhouette: silver-grey crooked tree along a steppe river

growth.juvenile_note: Seeds sprout in spring after a winter's chill. The seedling is a slim thorny shoot with narrow silvery leaves; it grows fast in moist sand and silt and soon branches into a crooked, often leaning, many-stemmed small tree with dark fissured bark and thorn-tipped twigs.
growth.source: USDA FEIS Elaeagnus angustifolia (tree to 12 m; fruits from 3-5 yr; seeds need cold stratification; tolerates shade, salt and drought; lives ~60-100 yr); Flora of China. Height curve estimated.

fruiting.source: USDA FEIS and Flora of China Elaeagnus angustifolia (fragrant bell-shaped flowers, silvery outside and yellow inside, May-June; dry mealy silvery-yellow drupes 1-1.5 cm ripen Aug-Oct and persist into winter; eaten by birds and people). Crop estimated.

bark.notes: dark grey-brown bark in shallow fissures, shredding in strips; twigs silvery with sharp thorns

leaf.notes: narrow silvery-grey willow-like leaves, scaly and almost white beneath

flower.form: small fragrant bells, silver outside and yellow inside, along the twigs

appearance.silhouette: pale silver crowns lining a river through the grass
appearance.refs: Kew POWO; Flora of China; USDA FEIS

canopy.name: Black poplar
canopy.source: Populus nigra, black poplar, Europe to W Asia, riverine floodplain woodland on gravel and sand, 20-30 m — Wikipedia / EUFORGEN

traits.native_range: Populus nigra, black poplar, Europe to W Asia, riverine floodplain woodland on gravel and sand, 20-30 m — Wikipedia / EU
traits.leaf_shape: simple or compound broad leaves, most deciduous in cold bands
traits.trunk: single trunk dividing into a rounded crown
traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

leaf.note: rhombic-ovate to deltoid, crenate-serrate, glossy, on flattened petioles

bark.note: dark grey-brown, deeply furrowed, trunk studded with large burrs

canopy.silhouette: broad heavy dome on a burred leaning trunk

growth.juvenile_note: Seed germinates within a day or two on fresh, wet river gravel and silt after the spring floods. Seedlings and saplings form dense thickets of slender single stems with glossy, diamond- to triangular-ovate, finely toothed leaves on flattened stalks that tremble; young shoots are often reddish. Broken branches and toppled trunks root readily, so many young trees are clones.
growth.source: JRC European Atlas of Forest Tree Species (to 40 m and 200 cm dbh; mature trees live 100, occasionally 300-400 yr; light-demanding pioneer, fast growing, wind pollinated, flowers before the leaves); Wikipedia (20-30 m, rarely 40 m). Germination and age at first flowering estimated from Populus.

fruiting.source: JRC Atlas (flowers before leaves; wind pollinated; fluffy seeds from capsules in catkins, spread by wind and water). Colour is the crimson male catkins. Catkin and capsule sizes, ripening (seed shed May-June) and crop estimated from Populus deltoides and other poplars.

shrub.name: Siberian pea shrub
shrub.source: Caragana arborescens, Siberia/Mongolia steppe and forest-steppe, legume shrub 2-5 m, yellow flowers — Flora of China

traits.native_range: Caragana arborescens, Siberia/Mongolia steppe and forest-steppe, legume shrub 2-5 m, yellow flowers — Flora of China
traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

shrub.silhouette: upright twiggy shrub, yellow pea flowers

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal: two thick oval cotyledons, then small even-pinnate leaves of 4-6 pairs of rounded leaflets. Seedlings reach about 30 cm in the first year and soon send up several stems from the base, forming an upright, open, multi-stemmed shrub with grey-green bark and paired spines at the leaf bases.
growth.source: USDA Woody Plant Seed Manual (Caragana: to 7 m, seed-bearing at 3-5 yr, flowers Apr-Jun, pods ripen Jun-Jul, 2.5-5 cm with ~6 seeds, split at once, dispersal done by mid-Aug; germination 5-21 days); NDSU extension (medium growth, long-lived, full sun); Alaska ACCS (grows in deciduous understories)

fruiting.source: USDA Woody Plant Seed Manual (yellow bisexual flowers Apr-Jun; pods green to amber/brown Jun-Jul, 2.5-5 cm, ~6 seeds 2.5-4 mm; pods split explosively as soon as ripe); Alaska ACCS (pods 3.5-6 cm, flowers single or in small groups); PFAF (seeds and young pods eaten cooked)

shrub.name: Steppe spiraea
shrub.source: Spiraea hypericifolia, Eurasian steppe shrub 0.5-1.5 m, white flowers — Flora of China

traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

shrub.silhouette: arching wands of small leaves, white-flowered

growth.juvenile_note: Seedling: tiny epigeal cotyledons, then a thin wiry stem with small obovate grey-green leaves. Within 2-3 years it branches from the base into a little twiggy bush of arching brown stems, and spreads by root suckers into low steppe thickets that are smothered in small white flower clusters along last year's shoots.
growth.source: USDA Woody Plant Seed Manual, Spiraea (seed germinates readily with little or no pretreatment; follicles split Aug-winter); Chicago Botanic Garden (May-Jun bloom on old wood); Flora of China/steppe floras (0.5-1.5 m, sessile umbels); timings estimated from the genus

fruiting.source: USDA Woody Plant Seed Manual, Spiraea (5 small follicles per flower, straw-coloured when ripe, split down one side; Virginia spirea follicles dehisce Aug-late winter); Trees and Shrubs Online (flowers under 1 cm); counts and timings estimated

shrub.name: Steppe wormwood
shrub.source: Artemisia austriaca, Eurasian steppe from Austria to Kazakhstan, silver sub-shrub 20-50 cm — Euro+Med PlantBase

traits.native_range: Artemisia austriaca, Eurasian steppe from Austria to Kazakhstan, silver sub-shrub 20-50 cm — Euro+Med PlantBase
traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

growth.juvenile_note: Seedling: two tiny oval cotyledons, then finely divided, silky silver-grey leaves in a small rosette. It becomes a low, woody-based subshrub that creeps by rhizomes into silvery patches of short upright shoots with feathery leaves, topped in late summer by sprays of tiny nodding yellowish flower heads.
growth.source: Wikipedia (native range Europe to W Siberia and Iran) with the description estimated from floras as recalled (Flora of the USSR: rhizomatous silvery subshrub 20-60 cm of steppe and overgrazed pasture, flowering Jul-Sep with tiny wind-pollinated heads) and seed biology of related steppe Artemisia.

fruiting.source: Estimated from floras as recalled (tiny globose yellowish heads 2-3 mm in narrow panicles, Jul-Sep; achenes ~1 mm ripen Sep-Oct) and wind pollination typical of Artemisia; crop and timings estimated.

shrub.name: Dwarf almond
shrub.source: Prunus tenella (Amygdalus nana), the steppe almond: a suckering shrub 0.5-1.5 m forming thickets in the feather-grass steppes from central Europe and Ukraine to western Siberia and Kazakhstan, smothered in pink flowers in April — Kew POWO / Flora of the USSR

leaf.note: narrow lance-shaped leaves, sharply toothed, glossy dark green

shrub.silhouette: low thicket of thin stems, pink in spring

growth.juvenile_note: Seeds need a cold winter in the ground before they sprout. Seedlings are thin reddish stems with glossy, sharply toothed narrow leaves; from the second or third year root suckers come up around the parent, so a single plant spreads into a low, open thicket of upright stems that flowers before or with the leaves.
growth.source: Kew POWO and Flora of the USSR (Amygdalus nana: shrub 0.5-1.5 m, suckering, flowers Apr-May, fruit ripens Jul); Wikipedia Prunus tenella. Germination and ages estimated from Prunus.

fruiting.source: Flora of the USSR / Kew POWO Prunus tenella (bright pink flowers 2-3 cm in April-May; velvety grey-green dry drupe 1.5-2.5 cm that splits to release a bitter, cyanogenic stone, ripe in July). Set and crop estimated.

bark.notes: smooth reddish-grey stems with horizontal lenticels

leaf.notes: narrow glossy dark green leaves with sharp teeth

flower.form: bright pink five-petalled flowers crowding the bare stems

appearance.seasonal: deciduous; pink flowers April, orange-red in autumn
appearance.silhouette: knee-high thickets blushing pink across spring steppe
appearance.refs: Kew POWO; Flora of the USSR; Wikipedia

ground.name: Crested wheatgrass
ground.source: Agropyron cristatum, Central Asian and Siberian steppe, 0.3-0.9 m — Flora of China

traits.native_range: Agropyron cristatum, Central Asian and Siberian steppe, 0
traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

ground.silhouette: green grass clump with flat comb spikes

growth.juvenile_note: Seedling: a single thin blade on unusually long, fast roots, so it establishes quickly. By its first autumn it is a tight tuft of several tillers with flat, slightly hairy, blue-green leaves; from the second year it sends up stiff stems topped by flat, comb-like spikes whose spikelets stick out sideways like fish bones.
growth.source: USDA FEIS Agropyron cristatum: germinates at 5-30 C after >=5 d dormancy break; seedlings very hardy and vigorous with long quick-growing roots; culms 25-100 cm; Alberta heading Jun 8, flowering Jun 29, seed ripe Jul 30; stands productive >30 yr (one >40 yr). NRCS plant guide: culms 30-90 cm. First-seed year and tuft size estimated.

ground.name: Feather grass
ground.source: Stipa pennata, dominant Eurasian steppe grass, feathery silver awns, 0.4-0.9 m — Euro+Med PlantBase

traits.native_range: Stipa pennata, dominant Eurasian steppe grass, feathery silver awns, 0
traits.leaf_shape: narrow grass blades in a dense tussock
traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

ground.silhouette: tuft trailing long feathery silver awns

growth.juvenile_note: Seedling: one or two very narrow, inrolled leaves after the long-awned grain screws itself into the soil; builds a small tuft slowly and flowers only after several years. Mature: a dense tussock of fine, rolled grey-green leaves topped in early summer by silvery, feathery awns 20-35 cm long that wave like plumes.
growth.source: Wikipedia Stipa pennata (60-90 cm, Eurasian steppe from Mongolia to Hungary, silvery plumes in summer); Flora Europaea (plumose awns 25-35 cm); flowering age and tussock lifespan estimated from steppe Stipa ontogeny studies

ground.name: Valais fescue
ground.source: Festuca valesiaca, Eurasian steppe bunchgrass, blue-grey, 20-50 cm — Euro+Med PlantBase

traits.native_range: Festuca valesiaca, Eurasian steppe bunchgrass, blue-grey, 20-50 cm — Euro+Med PlantBase
traits.leaf_shape: narrow grass blades in a dense tussock
traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

growth.juvenile_note: Thread-leaved seedling becomes a dense tuft of very fine, bristle-like bluish (glaucous) leaves, forming a compact low steppe tussock within a few years; flowers from year 2 in early summer and survives summer drought by going dormant.
growth.source: Estimated from Festuca valesiaca steppe ecology and Festuca ovina-group grasses (Grime et al. Comparative Plant Ecology for F. ovina).

ground.name: Parasol mushroom

repro.note: The mycelium is the organism and lives in the substrate for years; the mushroom is a days-long fruiting body. 'rhizome' here = the mycelium spreading through connected dead wood or litter; 'wind' = spores.

ground.source: temperate meadow and open wood; Tall drumstick then a parasol; grassland edges.. Standard mycological references (Kew POWO/Index Fungorum for the name).

traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

cap.form: egg then flat parasol cap, cream with concentric brown scales and brown umbo
cap.notes: cream parasol with shaggy brown scales, tall stem with brown snakeskin banding and a moveable ring

appearance.habit: scattered in grass and open wood
appearance.seasonal: fruits seasonally then rots or persists (brackets)
appearance.silhouette: tall drumsticks opening to wide parasols in a meadow

ground.name: June grass
ground.source: Koeleria macrantha (K. cristata), Poaceae: a cool-season bunchgrass 0.2-0.6 m of steppe and prairie across Eurasia and North America, with dense shining spike-like panicles in early summer — Kew POWO / USDA FEIS / Flora of China

leaf.note: narrow flat or inrolled grey-green blades, mostly basal

ground.silhouette: small grey-green tuft, shiny spike-like heads

growth.juvenile_note: Seedlings make a small, fine tuft of grey-green leaves in their first season. From the second year the tuft sends up slender stems topped by dense, shining, spike-like silvery-green panicles that open briefly in bloom and then close again, ripening straw-coloured by midsummer.
growth.source: USDA FEIS Koeleria macrantha (C3 perennial bunchgrass 20-60 cm, circumboreal in steppe and prairie, flowers early summer, establishes readily from seed); Kew POWO. Lifespan estimated.

leaf.notes: fine grey-green basal blades in a dense small tuft

flower.form: dense shining spike-like panicles 4-12 cm, silvery-green turning straw

appearance.seasonal: green in spring, straw by midsummer
appearance.silhouette: small grey-green tuft, shiny spike-like heads
appearance.refs: Kew POWO; USDA FEIS; Flora of China

ground.name: Grey-cushioned grimmia

growth.juvenile_note: Spores sprout into a green thread-web on bare rock and bud a few tiny upright shoots, which grow outward in all directions at the same rate so the clump becomes a perfect little dome. It grows only while wet and stays grey and hoary when dry; old cushions crowd into grey mosaics across a sunny boulder.
growth.source: BBS field guide and Flora of North America (cushions 1-2 cm high, leaves with long hyaline awns, setae arcuate burying the capsules in the cushion; on calcareous and acid rock and walls). Growth and ages estimated from moss biology.

repro.note: spores by wind and water; no flowers; dries out and revives with rain, so spread reads moisture not pollinators

ground.source: Grimmia pulvinata, Grimmiaceae: neat round grey cushions 1-4 cm across and 1-2 cm high on sunny rock outcrops, walls and stones, hoary with long silver hair points; capsules on curved stalks tucked into the cushion — British Bryological Society field guide / Flora of North America vol. 27

leaf.notes: lance-shaped leaves each ending in a long silver hair point, giving a hoary grey look

appearance.seasonal: grey and hoary when dry, darker green when wet
appearance.silhouette: round hoary grey cushions on sunny rock
appearance.refs: British Bryological Society field guide; Flora of North America vol. 27

fruit.form: small ribbed capsules on curved stalks nestled into the cushion

ground.silhouette: round hoary grey cushions on sunny rock

ground.name: Bristly haircap

growth.juvenile_note: Spores sprout into a green thread-web on bare sand that buds short stiff shoots; underground rhizoids send up more shoots so a patch spreads into a carpet. Shoots look like tiny grey-green bottlebrushes tipped with white hairs; in spring the male shoots open into red, flower-like rosettes.
growth.source: BBS field guide and Flora of North America (shoots 1-4 cm, leaves with long hyaline awns, male cups red; on dry sandy and gravelly ground, pioneer on burnt and disturbed sand). Growth and ages estimated from Polytrichum.

repro.note: spores by wind and water; no flowers; dries out and revives with rain, so spread reads moisture not pollinators

ground.source: Polytrichum piliferum, Polytrichaceae: short stiff shoots 1-5 cm with grey-green leaves ending in white hair points, in carpets on dry sand and gravel, sandy steppe and rock; male shoots end in red splash-cups — British Bryological Society field guide / Flora of North America vol. 27

leaf.notes: stiff narrow leaves crowded at the shoot tips, each with a white hair point, so the carpet looks frosted

appearance.seasonal: frosted grey when dry; red male splash-cups in spring
appearance.silhouette: grey-green bristly carpet on dry sand
appearance.refs: British Bryological Society field guide; Flora of North America vol. 27

fruit.form: four-angled capsules under hairy caps on red-brown stalks

ground.silhouette: grey-green bristly carpet on dry sand

ground.name: Steppe lichen
ground.origin: Steppes of Eurasia and North America

growth.juvenile_note: Rarely from spores; nearly always from wind-blown fragments that lodge between grass clumps. A fragment keeps growing at its lobe tips without ever attaching, curling into a loose, springy, tangled ball that drifts across bare ground with the wind and piles up in hollows.
growth.source: Brodo et al., Lichens of North America; Hale 1990, A synopsis of Xanthoparmelia (vagrant, lobes 1-2 mm wide, canaliculate, yellow-green to grey with usnic acid; Eurasian and North American steppe). Growth and ages estimated from foliose lichens.

repro.note: no flowers: spreads as unattached fragments rolled by the wind; spores rare; grows only when wet

ground.source: Xanthoparmelia camtschadalis, Parmeliaceae: a vagrant foliose lichen of steppe and dry grassland, narrow yellowish-grey lobes rolled into tubes and curled into loose cushions 2-5 cm that lie unattached on the soil and roll in the wind — Index Fungorum; Brodo, Lichens of North America; Hale 1990

leaf.notes: narrow strap-like lobes, yellowish-grey above and dark brown beneath, rolled into tubes and tangled into loose balls

appearance.seasonal: paler and brittle when dry, greener when wet
appearance.silhouette: loose pale yellow-grey curls lying on bare steppe soil
appearance.refs: Brodo et al., Lichens of North America; Index Fungorum

ground.silhouette: loose pale yellow-grey curls lying on bare steppe soil

ground.source: Pleurotus eryngii, Pleurotaceae: the steppe or king oyster mushroom, a weak parasite and decomposer of the roots of Eryngium, Ferula and other Apiaceae in dry grassland from the Mediterranean through the Ukrainian and Kazakh steppes to Central Asia; cap 3-12 cm on a thick white stem — Index Fungorum; Zervakis et al. 2001

associations.name: Inter-Andean dry valley scrub

associations.source: Inter-Andean dry valleys and rocky slopes of Ecuador, Peru and Bolivia (about 1,500-3,400 m): columnar cacti — Trichocereus (Echinopsis), with Browningia and Armatocereus lower down — among Puya, Agave, Opuntia, Dodonaea and Schinus molle; seasonally dry montane scrub (Weberbauer 1945; Ostolaza 2014 Cactaceae of Peru; Josse et al. 2009, NatureServe ecological systems of the Andes).
associations._note: 1 Oct (Mike: Trichocereus must be in the game): the realm gate only lets an 'andes' species grow in a biome that hosts the andes realm, and no dry biome did (only cold puna and paramo), so no Trichocereus could grow on any planet. The trim fills the companions and ground with real inter-Andean species.
